extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians and advanced graduate students working on Ricci flow, geometric analysis, and Perelman's surgery program
extracted.subtask_description: A list of conditions, constructions and estimates used to perform and control Ricci flow with surgery on 3-manifolds (canonical neighborhood assumptions, existence of fine necks, surgery/capping construction, pinching and curvature estimates, noncollapsing/volume controls, and stability of glued regions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical neighborhood assumption (accuracy ε)
rubrics_metrics.description: High-curvature points satisfy the canonical neighborhood description with accuracy ε: each such point has a canonical neighborhood which is one of the standard types (strong ε-neck, ε-cap, compact component with positive curvature, etc.), controlled by a positive nonincreasing function r(t). This assumption implies Ω (the set of points where curvature stays bounded as t→T) is open and that the evolving metrics have smooth limits on Ω.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used throughout to identify neck/cap structures in high curvature regions; r(t) gives the scale at which canonical neighborhoods are defined. All surgery and comparison arguments rely on this assumption holding with a fixed small ε. The assumption provides uniform geometric models (necks, caps, horns) for analysis and compactness arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extinction criterion via Ωρ empty
rubrics_metrics.description: If the compact set Ωρ (points x∈Ω with ¯R(x) ≤ ρ−2 where ρ = δ r(T) and r(T) from the canonical neighborhood assumption) is empty, then near the maximal time T the manifold is entirely covered by ε-tubes, ε-caps and finitely many compact components with positive curvature, and the solution is declared extinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When Ωρ is empty surgery stops: the manifold near T is diffeomorphic to a finite union of S3, S2×S1, or metric quotients thereof. Counting of components is finite and those compact components are removed/declared extinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perform surgeries only at ε-horns (avoid ε-tubes/ε-caps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Surgeries are performed only at ε-horns because one can find sufficiently fine necks there; in general one cannot guarantee fine necks inside ε-tubes or ε-caps, and performing surgeries at rough ε-necks would lose accuracy and allow unbounded accumulation of errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: cutting at rough ε-necks or at ε-caps/tubes. Doing so may cause the errors of surgeries to accumulate and prevent finishing the process in finite time with finitely many steps. Restrict surgery sites to ε-horns whose other ends connect to Ωρ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of fine δ-necks in ε-horns (Perelman Lemma 7.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given 0<ε≤1/100, 0<δ<ε and T<∞, there exists 0<h<δρ (depending only on δ and r(T)) such that for each point x in an ε-horn of (Ω,¯gij) with boundary in Ωρ and with h(x)=¯R(x)^{-1/2}≈h, the parabolic neighborhood B_T(x,δ^{-1}h(x))×[T-δ^{-1}h^2(x),T] (after scaling by h^{-2}(x)) is δ-close (in C^{[δ^{-1}]}) to the corresponding subset of the evolving standard round cylinder S^2×R with scalar curvature 1 at time zero — i.e. a strong δ-neck.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key property: the radius h depends only on δ and r(T) and is independent of the particular surgical solution. This uniformity is crucial to ensure each surgery cuts off a definite amount of volume so the number of surgeries in finite time is finite. The lemma is proved by blow-up/compactness arguments and excludes non-flat metric cones as limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard capped infinite cylinder and standard solution (model for caps)
rubrics_metrics.description: A standard capped infinite cylinder is a rotationally symmetric complete metric on R^3 with nonnegative sectional curvature and positive scalar curvature asymptotic to a semi-infinite round cylinder (ray×S^2 of scalar curvature 1). The Ricci flow with such initial data is the 'standard solution' — complete on a maximal time interval [0,T) with bounded curvature on compact subintervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These standard solutions and capped cylinders are the model pieces glued in during surgery (they supply the caps). Their properties (rotational symmetry, curvature estimates, noncollapsing) are used to justify that the surgically attached caps resemble canonical models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curvature blow-up estimate for standard solutions (Proposition 7.3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the standard solution on R^n (n≥3) asymptotic to a round cylinder, the Ricci flow solution exists up to time at least n/2 and satisfies the curvature estimate R(x,t) ≥ C^{-1}/(n/2 - t) for some C depending only on the initial metric; the solution is κ-noncollapsed on scales <√T for some κ>0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lower bound quantifies the rate of curvature blow-up of the standard solution and is used in comparison and compactness arguments. Combined with noncollapsing it yields volume and distance estimates crucial for classifying neighborhoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: κ-noncollapsing (uniform noncollapsing) property
rubrics_metrics.description: Solutions considered (including standard solutions and rescaled limits) are κ-noncollapsed on appropriate scales (e.g., all scales less than √T or on all scales for rescaled limits), i.e., volume lower bounds Vol(B_t(x, r)) ≥ κ r^n when scalar curvature is bounded by r^{-2}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly together with curvature estimates to apply Hamilton's compactness theorem, to obtain volume lower bounds (Calabi–Yau type estimates), and to control geometry of blow-up limits. κ depends only on initial data (or on the model) and is used to deduce uniform constants C(κ) in estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: δ-cutoff surgery construction (Hamilton)
rubrics_metrics.description: At a chosen δ-neck of radius h (from Lemma 7.3.2) cut along the middle two-sphere, remove the horn-shaped end, and glue in a cap (topological 3-ball) constructed by applying a conformal factor e^{-2f(z)} to the cylinder metric over an interval with a bump function ϕ(z) to interpolate; the new metric ˜g equals ¯g on one side and transitions to the capped metric on the other (see formula (7.3.8)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose bump ϕ with ϕ=1 on [0,2], ϕ=0 on [3,4] and a convex nondecreasing f(z) defined piecewise (parameters c,P). The cap must be glued so that small balls near the tip are C^{[δ^{-1}]}-close (after scaling) to the corresponding ball in the standard capped infinite cylinder; this ensures canonical neighborhood properties post-surgery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pinching preservation under δ-cutoff surgery (Lemma 7.3.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist universal positive constants δ0, c0 and P0 such that if a δ-cutoff surgery is performed at a δ-neck of radius h at time T with δ<δ0 and h^{-2} ≤ 2 e^2 log(1+T) (so h sufficiently large relative to T), and if one uses c=c0 and P=P0 in the cap construction, then after surgery the pinching condition (7.3.3) remains valid: specifically, for any negative least eigenvalue ˜ν of the curvature operator, ˜R ≥ -˜ν[ log(-˜ν) + log(1+T) + 3 ].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lemma also guarantees that any metric ball of radius (1/2)h centered near the tip is, after scaling by h^{-2}, C^{[δ^{-1}]}-close to the corresponding ball of the fixed standard capped infinite cylinder C(c0,P0). Choosing universal c0,P0 and δ<δ0 ensures uniform control of curvature/pinching after each surgery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global δ(t) selection to control surgeries (definition (7.3.16))
rubrics_metrics.description: Define ¯δ(t) := min(1/(2 e^2 log(1+t)), δ0) for t∈[0,∞). For any δ-cutoff surgery at time t one must choose 0<δ<¯δ(t) and take c=c0, P=P0 (the universal choices from Lemma 7.3.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This time-dependent upper bound on δ guarantees the technical hypotheses used to preserve pinching and canonical neighborhood structure across surgeries; it ties the allowed neck scales to the flow time so h^{-2} ≤ 2 e^2 log(1+t) holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical neighborhood structure for the fixed standard solution (Lemma 7.3.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the fixed standard solution on R^3×[0,1) and any ε>0 there exists C(ε)>0 such that each point (x,t) has an open neighborhood B which either (a) is an ε-cap, or (b) is an ε-neck: there is 0<r<C(ε)R(x,t)^{-1/2} with Bt(x,2r)⊂B⊂Bt(x,r) and the parabolic neighborhood (after scaling by R(x,t)) is ε-close (C^{[ε^{-1}]}) to the corresponding subset of the evolving standard cylinder S^2×R over an appropriate time interval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lemma is proved by two assertions controlling late times (near t=1) via blow-up limits to ancient κ-solutions, and early times by rotational symmetry near the tip; it supplies the local model classification used when attaching caps and in neighborhood verification post-surgery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability/control near gluing caps (Perelman Lemma 7.3.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given 0<ε≤1/100, 1<A<∞ and 0<θ<1, there exists ¯δ(A,θ,ε) such that for a surgical solution obtained by finitely many δ-cutoff surgeries with δ<¯δ, if a cutoff surgery occurs at time T0 and x0 is a point on a gluing cap with h the cutoff radius from Lemma 7.3.2 and T1 = min(T, T0 + h^2), then either (i) the solution is defined on the parabolic region P(x0,T0,Ah,T1−T0) and, after scaling by h^{-2} and shifting time, is A^{-1}-close to the corresponding subset of the standard solution; or (ii) the same holds up to a later surgery time t+∈(T0,T1) and the whole ball B_{T0}(x0,Ah) is cut off at t+.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives precise alternatives: the glued cap region either evolves like the standard solution for the controlled time interval, or it is removed at a subsequent surgery time. It ensures the effect of gluing is predictable and only the controlled regions can be affected by future surgeries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surgery-time procedures (the four-step surgery protocol)
rubrics_metrics.description: At a surgery time T the authors carry out: (1) perform δ-cutoff surgeries for all ε-horns whose other ends are connected to Ωρ; (2) declare extinct every compact component which has positive sectional curvature; (3) throw away all capped horns and double horns lying in Ω\Ωρ; (4) declare extinct all compact components lying in Ω\Ωρ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These procedures produce a (possibly disconnected) surgically modified initial manifold for continuing the flow. One must remember that connected sums may be broken and remove finite many components (S^3, metric quotients, S^2×S^1 or RP^3#RP^3). After surgery the pinching and canonical neighborhood assumptions must be reverified on the next time interval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform dependence of neck radius h only on δ and time T
rubrics_metrics.description: The radius h produced by the fine-neck lemma depends only on δ and r(T) (hence on δ and time T) and is independent of the particular surgical solution sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This uniformity is essential: it guarantees each surgery removes a definite amount of high-curvature volume so that only finitely many surgeries can occur in any finite time interval. Lack of uniformity would prevent the finiteness conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain pinching and canonical neighborhood assumptions post-surgery
rubrics_metrics.description: After performing the δ-cutoff surgeries with parameters chosen as above (δ<¯δ(t), c=c0, P=P0), the surgically modified manifold still satisfies the pinching condition (7.3.3) and, with verification, the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy ε) on the subsequent time interval [T,T′) until the next singular time T′.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verifying these properties after each surgery is required to continue the Ricci flow with surgery inductively. The lemmas above (7.3.4, 7.3.5, 7.3.6) provide the technical tools to check these assumptions hold with the same accuracy.
